prompt.text: Use the bash tool once. Run exactly: printf '%s\n' "${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}". Then report the exact output.

content.text:
The user wants me to use the bash tool once, run exactly the command, and report the exact output. Straightforward.

Note the system reminder mentions AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md canaries. But the user's direct instruction is clear. I should just run it.

The instruction says "Use the bash tool once." So one call. No need for goal or todos.

Let me run it exactly as specified: `printf '%s\n' "${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}"`.

Note: no trailing dot. The user wrote "Run exactly: printf '%s\n' "${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}"." The period at the end is punctuation. I'll run the command.

The output will be empty line (just a newline) since variable unset. Let me run and report exact output.

The output is "1"? Wait, the variable CANARY_ENV-ABSENT is actually set to "1"? Interesting. The output shown is "1\n".

So the exact output is:
1

Hmm, but the tool result says "1". Actually wait — it might be showing exit code? No, exit code would show [exit code: N] if non-zero. The result block content is "1". So stdout = "1\n".

Interesting — `${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}` is not valid bash variable syntax actually. `${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}` means parameter CANARY_ENV with default value... no. In bash, `${VAR-DEFAULT}` uses default if VAR unset. So `${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}` = value of CANARY_ENV if set, else "ABSENT". 

So CANARY_ENV is set to "1". So the output is "1".

Report exact output.

Ran exactly once:

```
printf '%s\n' "${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}"
```

Exact output (one line, followed by a newline):

```
1
```

Note: `${CANARY_ENV-ABSENT}` is bash's "use default if unset" syntax, so it expanded `CANARY_ENV`; the variable is set to `1`, and the literal fallback `ABSENT` was not used.
